meaning.text: Ralston calls Moroz the Russian peasants' counterpart of 'our own Jack Frost'.
Ralston renders Moroz-Treskun as 'the Crackling Frost'.

appearance.text: The peasants say Morozko is an old man.
The peasants say Morozko is short, a little old man.
The peasants say Morozko has a long grey beard.
In a tale, Frost comes out of his ice hut as an old man who is all white.

scene.text: In the tale of the stepdaughter, Frost is met in winter, in the depths of the forest, under a tall pine that stands on a hill.
His coming is heard as a cracking in the firs as he leaps from fir to fir, snapping his fingers.
To girls waiting in the forest, his cracking sounded as if someone were coming with bells.
In another tale, Frost lives in a hut made of ice in the forest, covered with snow and hung with icicles.
The peasants say Morozko runs about the fields and the streets in winter, knocking.

behavior_habitat.text: To the Russian peasants Moroz is a living personage.
The peasants say the cracking frosts begin from Morozko's knocking.
The peasants say the rivers are bound with ice from his knocking.
If he strikes the corner of a hut, a log is sure to crack.
In some tales Moroz-Treskun, or Studenets, appears among the bogatyrs, and his breath produces a severe cold.
Moroz-Treskun saves the hero who is ordered into a red-hot iron bath: he goes in and breathes, so that the heat at once turns to cold.
In the bath, Moroz-Treskun blew in one corner and spat in another, and hoarfrost and icicles hung everywhere.
In the tale of the stepdaughter, Frost descends the pine above a maiden left there and asks her again and again whether she is warm, cracking and snapping his fingers more each time.
When the stepdaughter kept answering that she was warm, Frost took pity on her, wrapped her in furs and warmed her with blankets.
The stepdaughter was found next morning alive, with a good pelisse, a costly bridal veil and a pannier of rich gifts.
The stepmother's two daughters, who complained of the cold and cursed him, froze to death under the pine.
In a variant from the Kursk Government, Frost comes to a stepdaughter in the open plain intending to smite her and freeze her to death, and names himself 'Frost the Red-Nosed'.
In the Kursk variant, Frost, pleased by her wise words, throws a warm cloak over her and gives her robes embroidered with silver and gold and a chest with a rich dowry.
In the Kursk variant, when the stepmother's own daughter gives him no wise words, Frost grows angry and kills her.
In a tale, a peasant's wife blames Frost for a field of buckwheat found broken down.
Frost gives the peasant who seeks him out a magic cudgel and a self-spreading table-cloth.
In some variants of the tale of the North Wind who gives a peasant wonderful gifts, the Frosts take the place of the Wind and his brothers.
In another story, Frost threatens to freeze a peasant to death because he bowed more to the Wind than to the Sun and Frost.
Sometimes the people describe Frost as a mighty smith who forges strong chains to bind the earth and the waters.
By Russian belief, the frosts fly in on 9 November from the iron mountains.
A folk riddle depicts Frost as a mighty bogatyr equal in strength to Samson.

dealing_with_it.text: On Christmas Eve the oldest man in each family takes a spoonful of kissel, puts his head through the window and calls: 'Frost, Frost, come and eat kissel! Frost, Frost, do not kill our oats! Drive our flax and hemp deep into the ground.'

Afanasyev gives the custom on Christmas Eve and on Great Day, with a spoonful of kutya or kissel, the old man standing on the threshold of the passage or climbing on the stove and putting his head through the smoke window.
Another form of the call invites Frost to come and eat kutya and not to freeze the buckwheat.
Sometimes, after calling Frost three times to the kutya and waiting a little, they add: 'Not coming? Then do not come to the rye, the wheat or any crop!'
The Tcheremisses are afraid to knock icicles off their houses, believing that Frost would then grow angry and freeze them all to death.
In the Kursk variant, the girl who greets Frost with 'Welcome, Frost; doubtless God has sent you for my sinful soul' is spared and rewarded.

notes.text: origin: no opened page says where Frost comes from or who becomes one (the 9 November 'iron mountains' belief is about the frosts' seasonal arrival and is filed under behavior). Searched moroz, morozko, frost (Ralston), мороз, морозко, трескун, mother frost across all sources; opened ralston1873 pp.214-223, afanasyev1865 pp.318-319 and 583-585, afanasyev1868 p.52 and pp.703-704, ralston1872 p.254.
variants: the Kursk telling is a variant of a tale, not a regional description of the being, so no variant block; no source describes Frost differently by people or region.

related: no opened page links Moroz to another pilot creature. Ralston p.223 groups the Frost tale with the Vasilissa / Baba Yaga tale as stepmother stories; that is a tale-type link, not a link between the beings, so baba-yaga is not listed.

People term not in sources/peoples.json: 'Tcheremisses' (ralston1873:p.222; 'черемисы', afanasyev1865:p.319 footnote). No people row written. They are not a Slavic people; proposed handling as for the Tatars under the Kazan row: no people row, term kept in the clause text only.

Afanasyev (1865 pp.318-319) also reads hoarfrost and icicles as Moroz-Treskun's spittle and snowy clouds as his hair; this is his mythological interpretation, not a described body, so it is left out of appearance. Afanasyev's pp.583-585 interpret winter as a mythic smith; only the plain folk statements (the 9 November belief, the riddle) are used. The Ukrainian-language invocation on afanasyev1865 p.319 ('Морозе, Морозе! иды до насъ кути іисты') is not attributed to a people by the page, so no Ukrainians row was added.

afanasyev1868 p.52 repeats that Frost is still treated to kissel and kutya in the family (cross-referencing vol. I p.319) but its OCR reads 'небольшой въ семьѣ', so it was not cited; the custom is cited from afanasyev1865 p.319 and ralston1873 p.222. ralston1872 p.254 gives 'Bobbin Moroz', the Carpathian name for a season, not this being: not used.
